title: Count Inversions
description:
# Count Inversions

An **inversion** in a list is a pair of positions `i < j` where `nums[i] > nums[j]` - a pair that is out of order. Count how many inversions the list contains. (A sorted list has 0; a reverse-sorted list has the most.)

A list of `n` elements can have up to about `n²/2` inversions, so checking every pair is `O(n²)`. The efficient approach piggybacks on **merge sort** (divide and conquer): while merging two sorted halves, every time you take an element from the right half before the left half is exhausted, it forms an inversion with all remaining left-half elements.

## Input

One line of space-separated integers (possibly empty).

## Output

The number of inversions.

```
Input:
2 4 1 3 5

Output:
3
```

The inversions are `(2,1)`, `(4,1)`, and `(4,3)`.

## Think about

- A correct `O(n²)` double loop earns the same answer and is a fine first attempt. Then try the merge-sort version that counts inversions in `O(n log n)`.
starterCode:
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))

# TODO: print the number of inversions (pairs i < j with nums[i] > nums[j])
hints: A brute-force double loop is O(n^2); merge sort counts them in O(n log n).
During a merge sort, when you take an element from the right half before the left half is empty, it forms an inversion with every remaining left element - add that count while merging.

```
SORT-COUNT(A)
    if length(A) <= 1
        return (A, 0)
    (L, cl) = SORT-COUNT(left half of A)
    (R, cr) = SORT-COUNT(right half of A)
    merge L and R into sorted M; each time you take an element from R,
        add (number of elements still left in L) to a counter
    return (M, cl + cr + counter)
print the count returned by SORT-COUNT(nums)
```
